title.en: The King Smites the Captive: Sacrifice Before the God's Standard
title.zh: 王擊戰俘：於神旗之前獻祭

region.en: Abydos and Thebes, Egypt (the royal sacrifice reliefs)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯與底比斯（王祭浮雕刻壁處）

texts.period: 1st Dynasty ivory plaque of King Den (c. 3000 BCE) through reliefs of all periods (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. VI, 'Osiris and Human Sacrifice, and Funeral Murders'

summary.en: The iconography of royal sacrifice: on an ivory plaque from Abydos King Den (Semti) grasps a captive's hair and lifts the mace, behind him the jackal standard of Anubis or Ap-uat — the sacrifice is made to a god by the king; Amenhetep II 'slew seven chiefs with his own club... and hung their bodies, head downwards, at the bows of his boat', and the Palermo Stele records an annual festival called 'the smashing of the Antiu.'
summary.zh: 王祭之圖像：阿拜多斯出土象牙牌上，第一王朝王丹（塞姆提）執俘之髮、舉杖欲擊，身後為阿努畢斯/阿普-烏阿特之豺旗——王於神前獻祭；阿蒙霍特普二世『親杖誅七酋……以其屍倒懸於舟首』；巴勒摩石銘且記一年一度『擊碎安提烏人之祭』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient iconography discussed in Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Sensitive subject matter handled descriptively, as historical record.

passages.text: The cult of Osiris set a curb on the cannibalistic tendencies of the Egyptians, but it did not eradicate them, any more than it put a stop to human sacrifice and funeral murders. As far as the evidence goes it seems to show that, although the Egyptians ceased to eat each other generally, they ate their enemies on occasions, and that they certainly slew their enemies, especially those whom they regarded as belonging to inferior races, and offered them up as sacrifices to their gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. VI.

passages.text: Here Ten, a king of the 1st dynasty, better known as Hesepti, or Semti, in whose reign certain Chapters of the Book of the Dead were 'found', is seen in the act of sacrificing a conquered enemy. He grasps the hair of the enemy's head with his left hand, in which he also holds a bow, and is about to smash the skull with the mace which he holds uplifted in his right hand. Immediately behind the captive is a standard surmounted by a figure of a jackal, which represents a god, either Anubis or Apuat, and thus it is clear that the sacrifice is being made to a god by the king. This scene occurs over and over again in reliefs of all periods of Egyptian history.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI.

passages.text: We read on a stele of Amen-hetep II at Amada that the king 'slew seven chiefs with his own club when they were living in the country of Thekhsi, and that he hung their bodies, head downwards, at the bows of his boat.' When he returned to Thebes he hung six of these opposite the pylon of the temple of Amen, and the seventh he sent to Napata, in Nubia, to be hung on the wall of the city to terrify rebels.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI.

passages.text: This only can be the meaning of the festival which is mentioned on the Palermo Stele under the name of 'smashing of the Antiu.' The Antiu were the dwellers in the Eastern Desert and Sinai, with whom the early kings of Egypt waged war continually. It seems that one of them must have won some decisive battle, which was held to be of such importance that an annual festival was established to commemorate it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI.

title.en: The King Dances Before His God: The Tablet of Semti
title.zh: 王舞於神前：塞姆提木牌

region.en: Abydos, Egypt (the wooden tablet of King Semti/Hesepti)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯（塞姆提/赫塞普提木牌）

texts.period: Wooden tablet of the 1st Dynasty (c. 3000 BCE); Budge 1911, chs. II and VII

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. VII, 'Osiris and Dancing' and ch. II

summary.en: The earliest picture of Egyptian worship is a king dancing: on the tablet of Semti the god sits in his shrine on the top of a flight of steps under a canopy, and before him stands the king with paddle and flail, his back turned to the god — 'Dancing was, and still is, an act of worship in Africa, and Osiris, according to Diodorus, was a patron of dancers and musicians of all classes.'
summary.zh: 埃及崇拜之最古圖像為王之舞蹈：塞姆提木牌上，神坐於階頂棚下之龕中，王持槳與枷立於前，背向神而舞——『舞於非洲素為崇拜之儀；據狄奧多羅斯，奧西里斯乃舞者與樂師——男女皆然——之庇護者。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient iconography via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The top of a flight of steps, and above it is a canopy, supported in front by poles, similar in every respect to the canopy under which Osiris is invariably seen seated in later monuments. Before the canopy is a figure of a king wearing the double crown of the South and North, and holding in one hand a paddle, and in the other a flail. On each side of him are three signs, which represent objects that were associated with dancing. The king, I believe, is dancing, though his back is turned to the god, and this representation appears to be the prototype of all the scenes, down to the Ptolemaic Period, in which the king dances before his god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. II.

passages.text: Dancing was, and still is, an act of worship in Africa, and Osiris, according to Diodorus, was a patron of dancers and musicians of all classes, both male and female.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. II, citing Diodorus.

passages.text: The tablet on which the above scene is cut appears to be one of several on which the principal events of the reign of King Semti (Hesepti) were recorded, and to contain a list of the chief events of a particular year... The first event noted of the year was the performance by the king of some ceremony which was connected with the god who sat in a shrine placed on the top of a short flight of steps. The ceremony must have been a very important one, or it would not have been noted in this manner.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VII.

title.en: Osiris in the Moon: Twenty-Eight Years and Fourteen Pieces
title.zh: 月宮之奧西里斯：廿八年與十四塊

region.en: The moon of Egypt (the Utchau, where Osiris unites himself to heaven like Ra)
region.zh: 埃及之月（烏特紹，奧西里斯如拉而合於天者）

texts.period: Lunar theology of the late period; Plutarch De Iside 42-43; Book of Making the Spirit of Osiris (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. XII, 'Osiris as a Moon-god'

summary.en: Osiris is the power of the moon: on the new moon of Phamenoth the Egyptians celebrated 'the Entrance of Osiris into the Moon'; the liturgy hails the moon as 'bull, that groweth young in the heaven each day' and cries that when Osiris enters the Utchau 'the beings on earth flourish' — the Nile appears at his utterance; and Plutarch's learned circles explained his 28 years of reign as the moon's days and his fourteen torn members as the days of the waning moon.
summary.zh: 奧西里斯即月之力：法梅諾斯新月之節名『奧西里斯入月』；禮文呼月為『日日在天而復壯之牛』，且謂奧西里斯入烏特紹之時『地上萬物遂得繁育』——尼羅應其言而出；普魯塔克時代之學者則釋其廿八年為月之週日、十四塊殘軀為下弦月之日數。

sensitivity.note: Ancient lunar theology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: It is certain, however, that just as at one time the star Orion was regarded as his abode in the sky, and Sothis that of Isis, so at one period Osiris was identified with the moon. This fact was well known to Plutarch, who says that on the new moon of the month of Phamenoth, which falls in the beginning of the spring, the Egyptians celebrate a festival which is expressly called by them 'the Entrance of Osiris into the Moon.' He goes on to say that by Osiris are meant the power and influence of the moon, just as by Isis they understand the generative faculty which resides in it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. XII, citing Plutarch, De Iside 43.

passages.text: 'Thou risest into the sky, Thou art united [thereto] like Ra. The sailors in [thy] boat give thee acclamations. The mouths of the gods of the horizon rejoice, Their throats follow thee. The love of thee is in hearts, awe of thee is in breasts. As soon as thou enterest the Utchau, And unitest thyself thereto, The beings on earth flourish (or, become fertile).'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XII, from the Book of Making the Spirit of Osiris.

passages.text: The lines which follow add: 'The Nile appeareth at thy utterance, making men to live through the effluxes which come forth from thy members, making all cultivated lands to be green by thy coming, great source of things which bloom, sap of crops and herbs. Lord of millions of years, sustainer of wild animals, lord of cattle; the support of whatsoever is is in thee, what is in earth is thine, what is in the heavens is thine, what is in the waters is thine.' Thus it is quite clear that Osiris was regarded as the Power of the moon, which produced the Nile-flood and therefore all the fertility in Egypt.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XII.

passages.text: Plutarch says that Osiris lived or reigned twenty-eight years, and thinks that the number twenty-eight manifestly alludes to the number of days in which the moon runs her course round the earth. He also refers to the ceremony which is performed at the funeral of Osiris, when a tree trunk is made into the shape of a crescent, and assumes that this symbolizes the waning moon. And he records the views of certain investigators who stated that the death of Osiris took place at full moon, and that the number of pieces into which his body was torn — fourteen — marks the number of days of the waning moon.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XII, citing Plutarch, De Iside 42.

title.en: Osiris the Bull: Apis Begotten by a Ray of Moonlight
title.zh: 牛神奧西里斯：月光之射所生之阿匹斯

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (seat of the cult of Apis; Heliopolis for Mnevis)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（阿匹斯祭之中心；赫利奧波利斯奉姆內維斯）

texts.period: Bull cult from the 2nd Dynasty (Manetho on Ka-kau) into the Ptolemaic period (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. XIII, 'Osiris as a Bull-god'

summary.en: The theology of the bull: kings are 'Mighty Bulls rising like the sun'; Apis is the black bull with the white blaze, the eagle on his back, double hairs in his tail, the beetle-mark on his tongue — 'begotten by a ray of light falling from the moon upon his dam'; at his death his soul joins Osiris to form the dual-god Asar-Hep, Graecized as Serapis; and in heaven the dead are promised a bull and seven cows of Sekhet-hetepet whose names the deceased must know (BD ch. 148).
summary.zh: 牛之神學：王皆自號『如日出於底比斯之公牛』；阿匹斯為黑牛白斑、背負鷹形、尾生雙毛、舌具蟲印——『月光之射落於其母而生』；其死則魂升而合於奧西里斯，成雙神阿薩爾-赫普，希臘化為塞拉庇斯；天堂中更有蘇赫特-赫特普特之牛與七牛，亡者須識其名（亡靈書一四八章）。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult history via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The kings of Egypt delighted to call themselves 'Bulls,' and one of the highest compliments the Court scribe could pay the king was to liken him to a 'young bull,' or a 'mighty bull.' Thothmes III describes himself as the 'Mighty Bull, rising like the sun in Thebes,' and the composer of the Hymn of Praise of him which is put into the mouth of the god Amen-Ra, says: 'I have made the people of Syria and Cyprus to see thee as a young bull, of determined courage, with horns ready to gore, indomitable.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. XIII.

passages.text: Apis was a black bull, with a white blaze on his forehead; on his back was the figure of an eagle, in his tail were double hairs, and on his tongue a beetle... The Egyptians connected Apis, both living and dead, with Osiris. He was the son of Osiris, as well as of Ptah, and was the 'living image of Osiris'; he was said to have been begotten by a ray of light falling from the moon upon his dam. After the death of his body, his soul was thought to go to heaven, where it joined itself to Osiris, and formed with him the dual-god Asar-Hepi, or Osiris-Apis. Early in the Ptolemaic Period the Greeks ascribed to this dual god the attributes of Pluto or Hades, and Graecized the Egyptian names under the form 'Serapis.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIII.

passages.text: In the Theban Recension of the Book of the Dead we find such passages as these: 'Homage to thee, Bull of Amentet,' 'Hail, Bull of Amentet,' 'Osiris, Bull of Amentet,' 'Thou art raised up, O Bull of Amentet.' As, according to one view, the Egyptians hoped to eat bull's flesh and to drink milk in the Other World, they assumed the existence in Sekhet-hetepet of a bull and seven cows, but to obtain the gifts of these creatures it was necessary for the deceased to know their names, which were supplied by the CXLVIIIth Chapter of the Book of the Dead.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIII.

title.en: The Ka, the Double: The Statue in the Niche

region.en: Egyptian tombs (the Ka statue behind the stone partition)
region.zh: 埃及陵墓（石壁之後的卡像）

texts.period: Doctrine attested from the Pyramid Texts onward (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XIX, 'The Ka or Double'

summary.en: Egypt's soul-anatomy begins with the Ka: born with every healthy child, an abstract individuality whose abode is the body — the 'DOUBLE'; when the body dies the Ka lives on, and a statue is made for it in the tomb, sometimes behind a stone partition with an opening, so the Ka may see and hear all that goes on when visitors come; it consumes not the bread and beer but 'only the spirits, or doubles, of the bread, beer, vegetables, meat, oil.'
summary.zh: 埃及靈魂解剖自『卡』始：凡健全之嬰皆伴生一抽象個體，居於身而導其行——即『兩重者』；身死而卡不滅，陵中為之造像，或置於有孔石壁之後，使卡得以視聽祭者之來；彼所食非餅與酒之實體，乃『餅酒菜肉油之靈，即其兩重者』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient doctrinal synthesis via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When the body was born there came into existence with it an abstract individuality or spiritual being, which was wholly independent and distinct from the physical body, but its abode was the body, whose actions it was supposed to direct, and guide, and keep watch over, and it lived in the body until the body died. No healthy child was ever born without this spiritual being, and when the Egyptians drew pictures of it they always made it resemble the body to which it belonged; in other words, they regarded it as its 'DOUBLE.' Its name in Egyptian was KA, and the hieroglyph which represents it is two human arms extended at right angles to the breast as if ready to embrace someone.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XIX.

passages.text: When the body died the Ka did not die with it, but continued its existence... The Egyptians prepared a figure or statue of the dead person to whom the Ka belonged, taking great pains to give it all the characteristics of the deceased, so that the Ka might recognize it as an image of its body and be pleased to enter into the figure and take up its abode there. The Egyptians placed the figure or statue so prepared in the tomb with the body, sometimes in a niche, and sometimes in a very small chamber behind a stone partition with an opening in it, so that the Ka might see and hear all that was going on in the tomb when visitors came there to pay visits in its honour.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIX.

passages.text: Not only was it necessary to provide a figure for the Ka to dwell in, but if it was not to perish of cold, hunger, and thirst, offerings of meat, drink, clothing, etc., must be placed in the tomb by the friends and relatives of the dead, so that the Ka might eat and drink, anoint and dress itself, even as its body had done when upon earth. The Ka did not, of course, consume the actual offerings of food which were given to it, but only the spirits, or 'doubles,' of the bread, beer, vegetables, meat, oil, etc., and similarly it arrayed itself in the spirits of the suits of linen.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIX.

title.en: Four Million Six Hundred Thousand Spirit-Souls
title.zh: 四百六十萬零一千二百之靈

region.en: The Tuat, Egyptian Other World (population of the spirit-land)
region.zh: 埃及冥界圖阿特（靈界之人口）

texts.period: Book of the Dead ch. 64, cited in Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XX, 'Spirits and the Spirit-World'

summary.en: A census of the otherworld: an obscure passage in the Book of the Dead mentions 4,601,200 (or 4,301,200) spirit-souls (khu); the spirits who reap the wheat and barley in the Domain of Osiris are nine cubits tall against five-cubit corn, and in the Fifth Division the spirits who live on the helpless shadows of the dead have thighs seven cubits long — 'Though naturally of a gay and light-hearted disposition, the Egyptian must have lived in a perpetual state of fear of spirits of all kinds.'
summary.zh: 冥界之戶籍：亡靈書一 obscure 段落載有『四百六十萬零一千二百（或四百三十萬零一千二百）之靈』；於奧西里斯之領刈麥者高九肘而麥高五肘；第五區以亡者之無助之影為食者，其股長七肘——『埃及人天性樂天，然必恆居於對諸靈之恐懼之中。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary cosmology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: An obscure passage in the Book of the Dead mentions 4,601,200, or 4,301,200, Spirit-souls (Khu), but whether these represented all the inhabitants of the spirit-world of Egypt cannot be said. In the Short Version of the Chapter '12 cubits' are mentioned, and this may be the height of the spirits. If so, spirits must have been of varying heights, for the spirits who reaped the wheat and barley in the Second Division of the Domain of Osiris were nine cubits in height, the wheat and barley being five cubits high. In the Fifth Division the spirits who lived on the helpless shadows of the dead had thighs (?) seven cubits long.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XX, citing Book of the Dead ch. 64 and ch. 149.

passages.text: Now, we read in many funerary texts of the 'Gods of the Tuat,' so we must assume that after death entered the world, and souls began to go to the Tuat, they found there these gods, who had been created by the unknown God... As time went on these gods became more and more independent, and the unknown God appears to have allowed them to do as they pleased, and in the end they became the arbiters of the destinies of the souls of men.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XX.

passages.text: Though naturally of a gay and light-hearted disposition, the Egyptian must have lived in a perpetual state of fear of spirits of all kinds.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XX.
